title: Source Diversity for Rare Cuneiform Sign Recognition
tagline: For a rare sign, is one more training example worth more if it comes from a new tablet?
abstract: Cuneiform sign-recognition models learn from crops cut out of photographed clay tablets, and rare signs may have only a handful of examples. Crops from the same tablet share a scribe, clay, lighting and photograph, so simply counting examples per class can overstate how much a model has to learn from. This project asks how much one extra training crop of a rare sign is worth for recognition on unseen tablets, depending on where it comes from: a tablet already in training, a new tablet, a tablet from another site, or an augmented or synthetic copy. It uses the public electronic Babylonian Library (eBL) Sign Snippets release, with tablet-disjoint splits, matched training conditions and paired seeds, and keeps a reserved test set untouched until the design is final.

stats.label: recall on unseen tablets when the same 8 examples per sign come from 8 tablets instead of 2
rare signs improved, with the gain holding in all 3 paired seeds
precision rose too: the model recognized the signs rather than just predicting them more often

compare.title: Recall on unseen tablets, same 8 examples per sign

findings: Same budget, more tablets, better recognition. Spreading 8 training crops per sign across 8 source tablets instead of 2 raised recall on unseen tablets from 12.7% to 19.5% for 30 Old Babylonian signs (ResNet-18, 20,891 crops from 337 tablets).
No cost elsewhere. Accuracy on the other 167 classes was unchanged (72.1% vs 71.8%).

The training protocol matters. With random initialization and a constant learning rate, the model barely learned the 8-example signs and the difference could not be distinguished from zero; the effect appeared with ImageNet-pretrained weights and cosine learning-rate decay.
Open question: part of the benefit may come from photographic variety, such as clay colour and lighting, rather than scribal hand. This pilot can't separate the two yet.

title: Conformal Prediction Under Distribution Shift
tagline: What happens to a coverage guarantee when the world changes, and what can restore it?
abstract: Split-conformal prediction gives regression models finite-sample, distribution-free prediction intervals with a guaranteed coverage rate, but the guarantee relies on the calibration and test data being exchangeable. This project asks a direct question: what happens to that coverage guarantee when the test distribution no longer matches the calibration distribution, and what can restore it? Using synthetic nonlinear regression data with a known ground-truth function, we build 90% split-conformal intervals, confirm they hit their target with no shift, and then introduce covariate, noise, and subgroup (mixture) shift. Every setting is repeated over 100 independent calibration/test draws. Coverage falls as low as 18%. We then evaluate a range of fixes: recalibration on shifted data, weighted conformal prediction with exact and estimated likelihood ratios, group-specific calibration, larger calibration sets, alternative base models, locally adaptive intervals (normalized scores and conformalized quantile regression), and, for streaming data, adaptive conformal inference (ACI) and rolling-window calibration. A single theme runs through the results: every method that restores coverage does so by spending interval width, and the methods differ mainly in how intelligently they spend it. Recalibration inflates widths almost sevenfold; weighted conformal stays valid but returns infinite intervals for most points under strong shift; normalized scores and group-specific calibration widen intervals only where the data are actually harder; and ACI combined with a rolling window holds 90% long-run coverage on drifting streams with no infinite intervals.

stats.label: coverage under strong covariate shift, against a 90% target (mean of 100 trials)
wider intervals needed to restore coverage by recalibration (4.08 → 27.65)
long-run coverage on drifting data streams with ACI plus a rolling window, and no infinite intervals

findings: Coverage must always be read next to interval width. Every method that restores coverage does so by spending width: recalibration widens intervals 6.8-fold under large covariate shift, and weighted conformal returns infinite intervals for most points.

Methods differ in where they spend width. Group-specific calibration and normalized scores widen intervals only for the points that are actually harder, holding coverage under mixture-type shift at a far smaller cost than generic recalibration. This requires the source of difficulty to be observable, as a group label or as a function of x.

Validity without labels has limits set by overlap. Weighted conformal needs no labels from the new distribution, and estimated weights work as well as exact ones here, but 16% of intervals are infinite at a shift of 1.0 and nearly all are from 2.5 on. It is a tool for moderate shift, not extrapolation.

When labels arrive over time, online correction works. ACI gives a long-run guarantee under arbitrary drift; combined with a rolling calibration window it holds 90% coverage with finite intervals in every streaming scenario, where standard intervals fall to 72–78%.
nextSteps: Move from synthetic data to a real dataset with a natural shift, such as a temporal or geographic split, to check whether these findings transfer.
Handle subgroup shift when group labels are not known, for example by clustering residuals or covariates to discover latent subgroups before calibrating per cluster.
Combine methods: normalized scores inside weighted conformal or ACI, so intervals adapt both to local difficulty and to shift.
Remove the need to hand-pick ACI's step size, and study delayed labels and periodic model retraining in the streaming setting.
Add diagnostics for weighted conformal, such as reporting the effective sample size, so a deployed system can flag when the calibration data no longer cover the test distribution.
